blocks.text: 1. Partitioning
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447162808-706928879.png
Partitioning covers how large collections get split for manageability and performance, moving from filtering queries to physically organizing storage.
It divides one large collection into smaller, more manageable physical pieces, a scaling technique used to keep performance predictable as data grows.
2. When One Collection Grows Too Large
A single collection can eventually grow too large for one index to handle efficiently.
Partitioning splits that one collection internally, without creating a separate collection.
3. Partitioning Versus Collections
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447163057-847091584.png
A collection is a logical grouping choice; a partition is a physical scaling mechanism.
The two concepts solve different problems, even though both involve splitting data in some sense.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Concept","Purpose"],"rows":[["Collection","Logical grouping of related vectors"],["Partition","Physical split within a collection for scale"]]}

blocks.text: 4. Common Partitioning Keys
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447163058-293034572.png
Date ranges, geographic region, or a hash of the vector id all serve as common partition keys.
The right key depends on how queries actually access the data.
5. Searching Across Partitions
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447163058-593056323.png
A query that targets a specific partition searches only that smaller piece.
A broader query instead needs to search across multiple partitions and merge the results.
6. Partition Pruning
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447163058-693002275.png
Similar to metadata filtering (Metadata Filtering), knowing a query's date range lets the system skip partitions outside that range entirely.
That skipping is called partition pruning, and it is a major performance win.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: A query filtered to the last thirty days never even opens partitions holding data from a year ago, thanks to partition pruning, saving substantial search time on a date partitioned collection.

blocks.text: 7. Load Balancing Across Partitions
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447163058-708976457.png
An unevenly sized partition can become a bottleneck that slows down queries touching it.
Choosing a partition key that spreads data evenly avoids that imbalance.

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: A partition key like recent date can create a hot, oversized partition for the current period while older partitions sit nearly empty, an imbalance that undermines the benefits partitioning was meant to provide.

blocks.text: 8. Partitioning As A Prelude To Sharding
Partitions can live on the same machine or spread across multiple machines entirely.
That distributed case, sharding, gets its own dedicated treatment as the next topic in this module.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Deployment","Description"],"rows":[["Partitions on one machine","Splits data logically, but everything stays local"],["Partitions across multiple machines","Splits data physically across a distributed system"]]}

blocks.text: 9. Recognizing When Partitioning Becomes Necessary
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447163059-232069880.png
Very large collections with natural access patterns benefit from partitioning.
Small, uniformly accessed collections rarely need partitioning at all.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Confusing partitioning with collections, using the wrong mechanism to solve a given problem.
Choosing a partition key that creates severely uneven, unbalanced partition sizes.
Never scoping queries to relevant partitions, missing the performance benefit of partition pruning.
Partitioning a collection that is still small enough not to need this added complexity.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: Partitioning divides one large collection into smaller, more manageable physical pieces.
A single collection can eventually grow too large for one index to handle efficiently.
A collection is a logical grouping; a partition is a physical scaling mechanism within it.
Common partition keys include date ranges, geographic region, or a hash of the vector id.
A scoped query searches one partition; a broader query merges results across several.
Partition pruning skips entire partitions that cannot match a query, a major performance win.
Uneven partition sizes can create bottlenecks, so choosing a balanced partition key matters.
Partitions can live on one machine or spread across many, leading into sharding.
Next up: Sharding, covering how partitions get distributed across multiple machines.
